summary: This document specifies requirements for an end-to-end session identifier in IP-based multimedia networks. It would let endpoints, intermediate devices, and monitoring systems identify one session across SIP devices, hops, and administrative domains.

eli5.summary: One call may pass through many phones and systems. This asks for a single ticket number that everyone can use to track it.

questions: what is an end-to-end session identifier
why is sip call-id not enough
what are the requirements for a sip session id
subtitle: What an end-to-end session identifier must do so one call can be followed across proxies, gateways and domains.

tldr.problem: SIP and H.323 each have a call identifier, but the two differ in syntax, B2BUAs often change the values, and transfers or joins lose the end-to-end link. A single call is hard to follow through a network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC does not define the identifier. It lists use cases and nine requirements (REQ1 to REQ9) that any end-to-end session identifier must meet, such as passing unchanged through B2BUAs and revealing nothing about users or devices.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document. It sets the target for a later document that specifies the actual identifier.

today: RFC 7206 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines requirements only; the identifier itself is to be specified in a separate document.

sections.title: Why Call Identifiers Fall Short
sections.content:
IP multimedia systems such as SIP and H.323 already have a globally unique call identifier meant to represent a communication session from the originating device to the terminating device. It is useful for troubleshooting and session tracking.

The RFC gives three reasons the existing identifiers do not work end to end. The syntax differs between SIP and H.323, so they cannot be exchanged across a network that uses both. Devices such as Back-to-Back User Agents (B2BUAs) often change the values as signaling passes through. And supplementary services such as a transfer, or a PBX joining two sessions, break the end-to-end property.

This document therefore specifies the requirements for an identifier that endpoints, intermediate devices and monitoring systems can use across multiple SIP devices, hops and administrative domains.
sections.eli5: Each switchboard stamps its own number on the call, and SIP and H.323 even write numbers differently. So nobody can tell which calls are really the same one.

sections.title: What Counts as a Session
sections.content:
The session identifier identifies a set of signaling messages associated with exactly two endpoints that, from each endpoint's perspective, relate to a single invocation of a communication application. What counts as one invocation is intentionally left loosely defined, because protocols and deployments define a "call" in different ways.

Acceptable sessions include a direct call between two user agents, a call through one or more SIP middleboxes, a call set up with third-party call control (3PCC), and the call that results when a user agent is transferred with a REFER or re-INVITE request. A conference through a focus, or an ad hoc conference run by one user agent, is not one session: each leg between two parties is its own session.

"End-to-end" means from the point of origin, through any number of intermediaries, to the ultimate termination. Legacy devices may not support the identifier, so an intermediary that does support it can inject one into the signaling.
sections.eli5: A session is one conversation between exactly two sides. A group chat is treated as several two-person chats, each with its own ticket.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC describes seven use cases. For SIP traffic with only proxies, the Call-ID header field is enough to identify messages in a transaction or dialog. That fails once B2BUAs or Session Border Controllers are in the path, so a single header field is needed that survives them. Messages in the same dialog MUST use the same session identifier.

  • Protocol interworking: a call from an H.323 endpoint through an SBC to a SIP user agent, or the reverse, MUST be identifiable end to end. The RFC expects the ITU-T to define H.323 protocol elements for this.
  • Traffic monitoring and logging: a provider's B2BUA changes header fields for privacy, so correlating logs from past days or weeks is hard without a common value.
  • Transferred sessions: tracking a call across transfers or joins until a BYE is sent.
  • Identifier syntax: a syntax that is too lax, with special characters or great length, is hard to encode in other protocols.
  • 3PCC: a controller that sets up a call between two user agents must produce a single identifier for that call. The case does not extend to three SIP user agents.
sections.eli5: The use cases are the situations where a shared ticket number helps: calls between different phone systems, finding trouble in old logs, and calls that get passed to someone else.

sections.title: The Nine Requirements
sections.content:
Nine requirements come out of the use cases. Four are firm MUSTs: the identifier must let a monitor tie together dialogs, transactions and messages of one session (REQ1), must allow correlating two sessions after a transfer or join (REQ2), must pass unchanged through B2BUAs and other intermediaries (REQ3), and must allow correlating sessions created by a 3PCC controller (REQ9).

REQ4 is about privacy. The identifier MUST NOT reveal anything about a user, device or domain, and it MUST NOT be possible to correlate identifiers produced over time with one another or with a user or device. The list of things it must not leak includes IP address, port, hostname, MAC address, username and the Call-ID.

REQ5 says traffic from and to devices that do not support the identifier MUST still be identifiable, for example by an intermediary injecting one. The SHOULD-level requirements are: unique in time and space like the Call-ID (REQ6), suitable for both SIP and H.323 (REQ7), and a restricted syntax and length (REQ8).
sections.eli5: The rules say the ticket number must stay the same all along, must work even when someone does not know about it, and must not give away who is calling.

sections.title: Work in the ITU-T and 3GPP
sections.content:
Because networks mix SIP and H.323, the RFC calls coordination across standards bodies imperative. A parallel effort in the ITU-T aims to introduce the session identifier for H.323 in a way that interoperates with the IETF procedures.

The Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) identified in Release 9 a need for a session identifier for operation and maintenance, to correlate flows in an end-to-end session. 3GPP TS24.229 notes that the identifier can correlate SIP messages of the same session even when B2BUAs are in the signaling path.
sections.eli5: Different groups write the rules for different phone systems, so they are working together to make sure the ticket number works for all of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Threats to similar SIP identifiers are documented in RFC 3261 and apply equally here. Storing the identifier in logs is also subject to the considerations of RFC 6872.

A badly built identifier could expose the person, device or domain behind a session. Following REQ4, the eventual solution MUST protect and obfuscate such information, and it MUST NOT reveal items such as a MAC or IP address. A second concern is spoofing: an attacker who duplicates an identifier could make diagnostic equipment unable to correlate messages. To prevent guessing and collisions, the identifier MUST be sufficiently long and random. Implementation details are left to the document that specifies the identifier itself.
sections.eli5: The ticket number must not say who is calling, and it must be hard to guess so nobody can fake it.

items.label: Identify session parts
items.desc: MUST let a monitor identify the dialogs, transactions and messages of one end-to-end session.

items.label: Transfers and joins
items.desc: MUST allow correlating two sessions when one is transferred or two are joined.

items.label: Pass unchanged
items.desc: MUST pass unchanged through B2BUAs and other intermediaries.

items.label: No identity leaks
items.desc: MUST NOT reveal user, device or domain information, or allow correlating identifiers over time.

items.label: Legacy devices
items.desc: MUST be possible to identify traffic from devices without support, for example by injection.

items.label: Unique
items.desc: SHOULD be unique in time and space, like the Call-ID.

items.label: SIP and H.323
items.desc: SHOULD be suitable for transmission in both protocols.

items.label: Restricted syntax
items.desc: SHOULD use a restricted syntax and length.

items.label: 3PCC
items.desc: MUST allow correlating sessions created by a third-party controller.
